passage: Our exams ran from the fourth to the fourteenth, and I watched Chaitanya prepare like someone laying bricks. A week before, he pinned a calendar above his desk: heavy days shaded red, one blank Sunday, and the four days after the last paper marked "nothing". During the exams he studied until ten and then switched off his lamp, even while the rest of us were still panicking in the corridor. On the blank Sunday he played football and came back muddy and hungry. When the exams were over, he slept, cooked with his mother and only opened a book on the fourth day, lightly. I cannot say what he was thinking. But he was the only one of us who walked into the last paper looking awake, and the only one who was not ill afterwards. Uma

qa.q: What did Chaitanya mark on the calendar for the four days after the last paper?
qa.a: The four days after the last paper were marked "nothing".

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been feeling when he switched off the lamp at ten while others panicked?
qa.a: Probably calm and confident in the plan, though Uma cannot be sure and only saw the behaviour.

qa.q: What could a panicking friend learn from Chaitanya's calendar?
qa.a: Plan the hard days with rest days around them, and put recovery on the calendar before the exams begin.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt watching the others panic while Chaitanya switched off the lamp?
qa.a: Probably a mix of admiration and envy, since Uma noticed Chaitanya looked awake and was not ill afterwards.

grounding: Illustrates a student who accepts an intense exam phase but schedules rest before and after it, seen by a classmate.

passage: On Tuesday, Sahil drew two columns on the whiteboard for the college fest. "Sprint for the last ten days, then a slow week after," he told Wasim, his co-organiser, and he blocked the Monday after the fest as a holiday for the whole team. On the Friday of fest week, Sahil ran the stage checks until midnight, went to bed at one, and refused Wasim's offer to stay until three. "Tomorrow is the real day. Be in by eight." The following Wednesday, the volunteers sat in the canteen at four o'clock, laughing and doing nothing. Sahil had answered only two messages all week, and Wasim finally had time to fix the banner properly, unhurried. "We'll do the same next term," Sahil said, tapping the whiteboard, where the slow week was still written in green.

qa.q: What did Sahil block as a holiday for the whole team?
qa.a: Sahil blocked the Monday after the fest as a holiday for the whole team.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably feeling when he refused to let Wasim stay until three?
qa.a: Calm and protective of the team's energy, wanting everyone fresh for the real day.

qa.q: What did the plan get right about the last days before a big event?
qa.a: It put the hard push into a short window and set a recovery week after it, so the team could repeat the effort next term.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt on the Wednesday with time to fix the banner unhurried?
qa.a: Relieved and rested, able to do the work properly rather than rushing while tired. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a thoughtful organiser who plans an intense phase for an event and a planned recovery week afterwards.

passage:
Binita, you're starting your final year? Let your Manoj mama tell you how I got through my CA finals without falling apart.
Before those exams, I made a calendar. Six weeks marked in red: that was the sprint. Ten hours a day, no cinema, no weddings, no cricket. I told everyone in advance. Your Nani was not happy.
But on the calendar, right after the red weeks, I had marked one full week in green. Sleep late. Visit friends. Do nothing useful. And inside the red weeks, every Sunday evening was off.
My friend Sunil didn't do that. He sprinted for four months without stopping. By the exam he was so tired he blanked in the first paper.
I passed. And I remember that green week better than the exams. I slept, ate your Nani's food, and played cricket till dark.
Plan the hard part, beta. But plan the rest too.

qa.q: How many weeks were marked in red on Manoj's calendar?
qa.a: Six weeks marked in red.

qa.q: How did young Manoj feel during the green week?
qa.a: Manoj felt relaxed and happy, sleeping, eating his mother's food and playing cricket till dark.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made Manoj's sprint work where Sunil's didn't?
qa.a: Planning a green rest week after the sprint and a free Sunday evening every week, so the effort could be sustained.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt when he blanked in the first paper?
qa.a: Sunil was probably exhausted and panicked, after four months of sprinting without rest.

grounding: An elder recalls a planned exam sprint with rest built in, contrasting it with a friend who sprinted without recovery.

passage:
Jatin's final exams started on the 10th. His sister Ankita's wedding was on the 26th. There was no way to move either.
He sat at the dining table with a calendar and a pencil. "Ten days, hard," he said. "Eight hours a day, nothing else. Then the exams. Then I stop."
Ankita laughed. "You'll be a zombie at my wedding."
"No. From the 22nd to the 26th, I'm off. No books. I'll sleep, help with the decorations and dance at your sangeet."
She looked at the calendar. He had even marked a half-day break on the 5th.
The sprint was hard. On the 4th he was irritable and snapped at their mother. On the 5th he took his half day and went to the market with Ankita.
He wrote his last paper on the 21st. On the 22nd he slept eleven hours.
At the sangeet, Ankita pulled him onto the floor. He danced like someone who had actually rested.

qa.q: When was Ankita's wedding?
qa.a: On the 26th.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel on the 4th?
qa.a: Jatin felt worn out and irritable, snapping at their mother during the sprint.

qa.q: What made Jatin's plan sustainable?
qa.a: Jatin planned a hard ten-day sprint but also a half-day break inside it and four full days of rest before the wedding.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel at the sangeet?
qa.a: Ankita feels happy and relieved, pulling her rested brother onto the dance floor.

grounding: Shows a young adult who accepts an intense exam phase but plans rest around it, keeping the effort sustainable.

passage:
In the Bengaluru co-working space, Tushar's team had just launched their college events app after a three-week crunch. Late nights, cold dosas at midnight, everyone sleeping four hours.
Anirban was already opening a new document. "Next feature. Let's start tonight."
Tushar shook his head. "No. Next week is light. Everyone works half days and leaves by three."
"We'll lose momentum."
"We'll lose people if we don't stop. Look at Neha." Neha was asleep on the beanbag with her laptop open.
Tushar pulled up the calendar he'd made at the start of term. The three weeks of crunch were marked, and so was this recovery week. So was the next crunch, before the fest in March.
"We sprint when it matters. We don't sprint all the time."
Anirban grumbled, but closed the document. On Monday of the next month, the team came back rested, and the new feature took half the time they'd expected.

qa.q: How long had the team's crunch lasted?
qa.a: A three-week crunch.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel about the light week?
qa.a: Anirban felt impatient and worried they would lose momentum, grumbling while closing the document.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's recovery week a wise choice?
qa.a: Tushar saw the team was exhausted and planned rest between crunches, so they came back able to work faster on the next feature.

qa.q: How might Neha feel about the light week?
qa.a: Neha would probably feel relieved and grateful, given she had fallen asleep on the beanbag.

grounding: Illustrates a leader who accepts intense launch phases but plans recovery weeks around them, keeping the team sustainable.

passage:
"You're making a calendar for the whole semester?" Nirmala leaned over Tenzin's desk.
"Just the shape of it. These three weeks in November are exams, so they're red. I'll study most of the day then. No football, no trips home."
"And after?"
"That week in green is the easy week. Sleep, football, call Amala, go home to Darjeeling. And the grey weeks before are normal: classes, two hours of revision a day."
"Last year you just went red from August."
"I know. By the exams I couldn't read a page without my eyes closing. And I fell sick right after."
"So red is allowed now?"
"Red is allowed if green comes after. The exams need the push. I just can't live in it."
Nirmala picked up a pen. "Make me one. My project deadline falls in the same week."
Tenzin grinned and pulled out another sheet. "Red, then green. Promise you'll actually take the green."

qa.q: Which weeks does Tenzin mark in red?
qa.a: The three weeks in November, when the exams are.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala ask Tenzin to make one too?
qa.a: Nirmala seems persuaded and hopeful, and perhaps a little worried, since a project deadline falls in the same week and the plan looks like it could help.

qa.q: What makes Tenzin's plan more sustainable than last year's?
qa.a: Tenzin allows an intense red phase only for the exams and plans a green week of rest right after, instead of sprinting from August.

qa.q: What would change if Tenzin skipped the green week again?
qa.a: Tenzin could end up exhausted and sick after the exams, just like last year.

grounding: Shows a student accepting an intense exam phase but planning easier weeks and rest around it.
